title: Balancing constitutional safeguards with effective government
label: 11 November 2026 · Constitutional safeguards
summary: Morgan McSweeney argued that democracy is threatened both when governments abuse power and when they fail to deliver their lawful plans, and that safeguards should protect against both risks. He called for Parliament to review the growing body of rules around prime ministerial power, keep necessary protections and clarify what government can do. Members challenged whether existing checks are strong enough and asked about the roles of Parliament, the Civil Service and the Cabinet. McSweeney also argued that better coordination and longer-term planning at the centre of government could help it act more effectively.

speakers.label: Morgan McSweeney
speakers.name: Morgan McSweeney
speakers.role: Former Chief of Staff to the Prime Minister, 10 Downing Street

glossary.definition: A guide describing how the UK Government and its main institutions are expected to work.
The rules and standards that government ministers are expected to follow.
Government decisions made under rules that require ministers to act impartially, which may limit consultation with colleagues.
A court process that checks whether a public body acted lawfully.
Established political practices that are generally followed, even when they aren't written into law.
The senior civil servant who leads the Civil Service and supports the Prime Minister and Cabinet.

chapters.title: Two risks to democracy
chapters.takeaway: McSweeney said democracy needs safeguards against both abuse of power and government failure.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You saw government working from the centre. Is the UK's constitutional democracy under threat, and what did you observe?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Democracy is always under pressure to show that it works for people. It can be threatened by abuse of power, but also when elected governments fail to deliver their lawful plans.

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Populists who want to undermine institutions can use that failure against them. In my view, failing to deliver can damage a government's legitimacy as much as abusing power can.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: What changes to the constitution would you like to see?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: There are many rules governing a Prime Minister's powers. Each may have been introduced for a good reason, but we should review them together, keep those that prevent abuse and ask whether the rest are justified.

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: I would also make the rules clearer, perhaps by updating the Cabinet Manual, so citizens and those in power understand the roles of the Prime Minister, Cabinet, Parliament and courts.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: Would it help to make the Ministerial Code legally binding?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: It might. When rules depend on individuals interpreting them in good faith, people can reach different conclusions about what a minister can or should do.

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: But first I'd review the whole collection of rules. Many were added after a mistake, and the extra reviews or pauses in decision-making have accumulated over time. Some may now make it harder for governments to deliver their lawful plans.

chapters.title: Keeping checks on prime ministerial power
chapters.takeaway: He wanted unnecessary obstacles reviewed, but said Parliament and other safeguards must remain able to stop abuses.

turns.speaker: Lord Beith
turns.text: Could a Prime Minister use the argument about delivery to weaken safeguards against abuse, claiming that getting things done is more urgent?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Any review or rewriting of the rules should be decided by Parliament, not by the Prime Minister. The courts, Parliament, Cabinet, civil servants, political parties and elections all provide checks.

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: A Prime Minister shouldn't be able to take Parliament's or the courts' powers, or violate people's rights. I'm not arguing for removing those protections. The rules should be clear and should protect against abuse while still allowing government to act.

turns.speaker: Lord Beith
turns.text: One safeguard survived all those checks: a previous government required the Electoral Commission to follow a policy statement from the government. A later government is now changing that.

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: I don't know enough about that example to comment. I have seen other rules interpreted in ways that leave a Secretary of State unable to discuss a decision with the Prime Minister or Cabinet colleagues, even when the decision affects several areas of government.

turns.speaker: Lord Griffiths of Burry Port
turns.text: How much does the constitution rely on people in power showing self-restraint and following unwritten practices? Can rules ensure that leaders have good judgment?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: We can't build a system that depends on having a trustworthy Prime Minister. Political parties choose candidates and leaders, and the public decide who governs at elections. Codes can't judge a leader's character.

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Clear rules help a Prime Minister know the limits of their power, instead of having to guess or receive conflicting advice. Cabinet members can also challenge a Prime Minister they believe is abusing power.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: If rules are interpreted in a way Parliament doesn't agree with, should the House of Commons act as a restraint?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Yes. Parliament can change laws, question ministers, hold debates and use committees to challenge a Prime Minister. If enough MPs believe the Prime Minister has overstepped, they can raise it.

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: It would help MPs to know clearly what the limits are. Different members can focus on different problems, so Parliament can challenge a Prime Minister even when individual MPs have to choose which issues to pursue.

chapters.title: Rules, ministers and civil servants
chapters.takeaway: McSweeney distinguished breaking the law from challenging established practice, and argued for clarity about when ministers can consult colleagues.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Can you point to rules that should be removed?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: I wouldn't single out individual rules. Each may seem reasonable by itself, but together they can leave a Prime Minister unsure what they can do and slow decisions down. The whole system needs reviewing by people who understand which rules are law, practice or precedent.

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: One area to examine is quasi-judicial processes. In some cases, rules seem to stop a Secretary of State discussing a decision with Cabinet colleagues or the Prime Minister, even when the issue is urgent and affects several departments.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: You mentioned judicial review earlier in a way that sounded like you thought courts had too much power. But judicial review is limited.

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: I misspoke. I meant quasi-judicial processes inside government, not court challenges. I was referring to rules that seem to prevent wider discussion of a decision.

turns.speaker: Lord Bichard
turns.text: Should civil servants see themselves as protectors of the constitution, beyond giving advice to ministers?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Yes, and in general I think they do give clear advice when they believe a minister is doing something wrong. But there's an important difference between a minister acting unlawfully and a minister departing from an established practice.

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: If a civil servant believes a minister is breaking the law, there are ways to raise that concern. But ministers should be able to question advice about how a rule or practice applies, and may sometimes want to change a practice if doing so is lawful.

turns.speaker: Lord Bichard
turns.text: What if a minister appears to be ignoring an important constitutional principle?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Usually, it shouldn't reach an open conflict. As chief of staff, I spoke regularly with the Cabinet Secretary to raise tensions or frustration and find a solution. Either of us could call the other if something became urgent.

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: The distinction still matters: a civil servant believing a minister is breaking the law is different from a minister disagreeing with a practice or precedent. A civil servant may sometimes have to carry out a lawful decision they disagree with.

chapters.title: How government can work together
chapters.takeaway: He argued that clearer powers, better coordination and more long-term planning could help government deliver without weakening safeguards.

turns.speaker: Lord Jones of Penybont
turns.text: When you were in Downing Street, how did you assess the constitutional effects of a decision?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: The rules were a constant part of the work. When a decision might be constrained, we would ask civil servants what the barrier was and whether there was a more effective way to make the decision.

turns.speaker: Lord Jones of Penybont
turns.text: What do you mean by quasi-judicial processes?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Sometimes a law says that a Secretary of State must make a particular decision. That can be interpreted to mean they must decide alone, without discussing it with Cabinet colleagues or the Prime Minister.

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: The Secretary of State should still make the decision where the law assigns it to them. But when it affects national interests or several departments, colleagues should be able to discuss it with them first.

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: When Keir Starmer became Prime Minister, he wanted to set priorities for departments and follow up with ministers on progress. At first, we were told that wasn't the usual practice. But a Prime Minister needs to give direction and coordinate the Cabinet; that doesn't mean taking decisions away from ministers.

turns.speaker: Lord Beith
turns.text: Should Secretaries of State lose their independence to make decisions?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: No. If the law gives them the decision, they should make it. My concern is when the rules are read to prevent them discussing a major decision with the Prime Minister or Cabinet colleagues beforehand.

turns.speaker: Lord Waldegrave of North Hill
turns.text: You said the centre of government was too weak. The Cabinet Office has grown considerably. What would make the centre work better?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Size and strength aren't the same. Government can be large but poorly organised. For example, departments have many communications staff, but they aren't centrally coordinated, so urgent issues can fall between departments while each handles its own press enquiries.

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Better coordination doesn't necessarily mean more staff; it may mean fewer. No. 10 also needs more time for long-term planning, so future challenges can inform decisions such as budgets and the government's programme.

chapters.title: Are Parliament and Cabinet strong enough?
chapters.takeaway: Members questioned whether political checks have weakened, while McSweeney said MPs and Cabinet ministers still have the ability to challenge leaders.

turns.speaker: Lord Cryer
turns.text: Checks through Cabinet and Parliament may be weaker than they were decades ago. Labour MPs used to elect much of their shadow Cabinet, and MPs can now focus heavily on constituency issues. Can those checks be strengthened?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: I can't compare directly with 30 years ago, but I saw MPs with a wide range of interests. On nearly every national issue, there were MPs who were well informed and wanted to question or improve government plans.

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: A Prime Minister also needs a Cabinet that commands respect across the governing party, so ministers with strong support among MPs still matter. Ministers and MPs can challenge decisions, often before legislation reaches Parliament.

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: No single safeguard can restrain a Prime Minister on its own. Courts, Parliament, Cabinet, civil servants, political parties and voters all play a part, and their combined effect matters. My experience was that many MPs were engaged in issues beyond their own constituencies.
